children.author: joefourier
children.text:
That's bonkers, you'd have to divide the market cap of SpaceX by the number of launches to get that figure, and that has nothing to do with the true cost anyway. By that same logic, the true of a Costco hot dog combo is about $140 ($470B market cap / estimated 3.4 billion hot dogs sold since 1985), Costco must be losing so much money selling it for $1.50!

Firstly, market cap isn't money "given", it's the value of all shares (including those still being held privately), and the actual money raised by the IPO was a small fraction of the total worth of the company. If you counted all the money that SpaceX actually got, it would be around $200B, so 200B/720 (the number of reported launches) gives about $300M per launch.

But that's still nonsensical because Falcon 9 was developed way before the IPO and financial shenanigans of the xAI/SpaceX merger, and you can't count the costs related to Grok, datacentres, Starlink, Starship, buying Twitter, etc. when estimating how much a launch costs. The whole Falcon 9 programme (including reusability) only cost about $2B to develop from what I could look up. Nobody is paying $3B to launch a Falcon 9 anymore than anybody is paying $140 for a Costco hotdog.

Given that both OpenAI and Anthropic are losing money FAST it's definitely the case. It's just that investors were willing to put up the cost, but now they want to see not just their money back, but a return on it. A return on about a trillion dollars, or about a 20x (2000%) rise in Anthropic revenue. OpenAI is still private, so unknown, but will be roughly similar.

It's like saying SpaceX launch cost is 44 million, self-reported. If you instead count the total amount of money given to SpaceX (debt + equity + govt) divided by the number of launches, a SpaceX launch costs about 3 billion dollars, roughly double the cost of a space shuttle launch.

One of those 2 figures is the true cost.

Subsidization implies that the subscriptions are offered at a loss; there's no reason to believe that is the case.  There is price discriminization at play, sure, but let's not buy the framing that the API price is the "right" price and subscriptions are some amazing giveaway.
